prayer.text: Saint John of the Cross, pray for us.

cues.text: Poverty and Early Life
Born Juan de Yepes in 1542 at Fontiveros in Old Castile, John was the youngest son of a silk weaver.
His father had been disinherited by his noble family for marrying beneath his rank, then died when John was still a small child, leaving the family in genuine poverty.
Educated at a charity school for orphans at Medina del Campo, John proved a diligent if unremarkable student who struggled, ironically, when apprenticed to a trade.

He entered the Carmelite order at twenty-one and was sent to study theology at the renowned University of Salamanca , where he was ordained a priest in 1567, already inclined toward the stricter, more contemplative Carthusian life.
Meeting Teresa of Ávila
Before John could transfer to the Carthusians, he met Teresa of Ávila , then fifty-two and already several years into her project of reforming the Carmelite order back to its primitive austerity.

Teresa, recognizing in the small, intensely serious young priest exactly the kind of collaborator she needed to extend her reform to the friars, persuaded him to remain a Carmelite and help found a reformed house for men instead.
On November 28, 1568 , John and two companions inaugurated the first monastery of what became the Discalced Carmelite friars .
They established it at a tiny, dilapidated house in Duruelo, living in conditions of poverty so severe that even Teresa privately doubted anyone could bear them for long.
Imprisonment and the Dark Night
The reform Teresa and John championed provoked bitter resistance from the unreformed "Calced" Carmelites, who saw it as an implicit rebuke and a threat to their authority.

In December 1577, Calced friars seized John, dragging him to their priory in Toledo, where he was imprisoned for nine months in a cramped, windowless cell, subjected to public lashings and pressured to abandon the reform.
It was during or shortly after this imprisonment — accounts differ on the precise timing — that John composed some of his greatest poetry.
He reportedly set down verses of the Spiritual Canticle from memory after escaping through a narrow window in August 1578.
That ordeal gave rise to the phrase for which he remains best known, the "dark night of the soul."
The Mystical Doctor
John's poetry and the prose commentaries he wrote to accompany it include Ascent of Mount Carmel , Dark Night of the Soul , and The Living Flame of Love .
Alongside the Spiritual Canticle , they form one of the most sophisticated treatments of the soul's purification and union with God in the entire Christian mystical tradition.
Teresa wrote from vivid personal experience in accessible, conversational prose.
John wrote as a trained theologian and poet, mapping with exacting precision the successive stages by which the soul is stripped of attachment to the senses and the intellect alike.
This process unites the soul with God in pure faith and love.
Legacy
In his final years John faced renewed hostility from within the now-separate Discalced reform itself.
He was effectively exiled to a remote, unhealthy priory in southern Spain, where he died on December 14, 1591 , still only forty-nine, worn down by illness and years of conflict.
Beatified in 1675 and canonized in 1726, John was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926.
His poetry, still studied as much for its literary genius as its theology, ranks among the summits of the Spanish language.
His account of spiritual darkness as a stage of growth rather than mere absence of God continues to console believers navigating their own periods of spiritual dryness.
